unit.title: Weld using gas tungsten metal arc welding process GTAW - (Tungsten inert gas -TIG)

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to weld with GTAW (TIG) to a procedure in all positions, on carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminium, including pipe. You will learn to choose and set the current, AC balance, frequency and pulse, prepare tungstens, choose gases, set up and check a back purge, weld open roots and fixed pipe, control heat and contamination, find and prevent defects, inspect and record the work, and lead others safely.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW)**, also called **TIG** (tungsten inert gas), at an advanced level: welding carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminium in all positions, including pipe; back purging; using AC balance, frequency and pulse; choosing and preparing tungstens; controlling heat; inspecting and recording the work; and leading others.

At Level 2 you welded plate and simple joints in the flat and horizontal positions. At Level 3 you weld to a procedure on pipe and in every position, set up purges and advanced machine functions, explain why each setting matters, and act as the team leader who checks other people's work.

TIG is chosen where quality matters more than speed: pipe roots for pressure and process lines, stainless steel for food, drink and hotel kitchens, thin sheet, aluminium boats and tanks, and repairs. In Jamaica you will meet it in food and beverage plants, hotels, water and sewage works, boat yards and engineering shops.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Plan to a procedure
Read the WPS, choose current type, tungsten, gas, filler and settings for the metal and joint; trial new procedures and keep the records.
Work safely and lead safely
Control UV, ozone and fume, tungsten grinding dust, HF interference, argon in low spaces, shock and cleaning chemicals.
Set the machine
Use DCEN and AC, HF or lift start, pre-flow and post-flow, slope, pulse, AC balance and frequency, and water-cooled torches and gas lenses.
Choose and prepare tungstens and gas
Pick the tungsten type and size, grind it correctly, choose argon or argon-helium, set the flow, use trailing shields.
Back purge
Set up dams, tape and vents, purge to the oxygen level the WPS gives, and keep the purge on.
Weld in all positions
Make open roots with a keyhole, walk the cup or weld freehand, and weld fixed pipe (5G, 6G) from the bottom to the top.
Weld stainless steel and aluminium
Control heat input and distortion, avoid contamination, clean heat tint, deal with oxide and porosity.
Inspect, test and record
Find and prevent defects, choose inspection methods, and keep weld and purge records.
Lead the team
Coach trainees, check settings against the WPS, deal with wrong materials, and leave the area safe.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on procedures, safety, machine settings, tungstens, gases, purging, stainless steel, aluminium, technique, positions, defects, inspection, calculations and supervision.
A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms (for example HF, back purge, oxide, ppm, heat tint, stick-out, purge dam, autogenous) and essays in full sentences, with any sums worked out.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: a TIG root and cap on a carbon steel pipe in the 5G position with a weld record and inspection; and TIG welding stainless steel sheet with a back purge, followed by inspection and heat-tint cleaning.

blocks.note: Learn the settings as **cause and effect**: what happens to the arc, the pool and the tungsten when you change balance, frequency, angle, pulse or gas flow. Most Level 3 questions describe what went wrong and ask you why.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: A clean, slag-free weld with very good control of the pool: ideal for **pipe roots**, thin sheet and visible welds.
Welds almost every metal: carbon and stainless steel, aluminium, copper, nickel alloys, titanium.
Heat and filler are controlled separately, so the welder can add rod only when the pool needs it.
It is slow. On thick pipe, TIG is often used for the root (and sometimes the hot pass), with MMAW or FCAW for the fill and cap.

blocks.note: **DCEN** (electrode negative) puts most of the heat into the work and keeps the tungsten cool: it is used for nearly everything except aluminium and magnesium. **AC** is needed on aluminium because the electrode-positive half of each cycle breaks up the oxide skin.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: The WPS, PQR and welder qualification

flow: Write a draft WPS: base metal and thickness, joint design and gap, filler and its size, tungsten type and size, gas and flow, purge, current type and range, position, preheat, interpass limit, travel speed
Weld a test piece to the draft, recording every setting actually used
Inspect it by eye, then test it as the job's standard says (bend tests, macro-etch, radiography)
If it passes, write the results and the real settings on a procedure qualification record (PQR), which supports the WPS
Approve and issue the WPS to the welders
Each welder passes a qualification test on that kind of joint and position; certificates are kept on file and checked to see they are current
On the job, each weld is recorded against the WPS and the welder's ID

ul: The WPS gives ranges. If a welder's setting is outside a range (for example 125 A when the WPS allows 80–110 A for the root), stop and put it right; the weld already made may need checking.
If the store does not have what the WPS lists (for example a different tungsten type), check whether the WPS allows a substitute. If it does not, get the right material; do not "make do".
Keep the **material certificates** that come with each batch of filler rod and plate, and record batch and heat numbers on the weld record.

Method
Worked example
rows: Heat input (kJ/mm)
Volts × amps × 60 ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1 000)
Time to weld round a pipe
Circumference ÷ travel speed
A 60.3 mm pipe has a circumference of about 189 mm; at 70 mm/min: about **2.7 minutes**
Gas in a cylinder
Flow × minutes of arc time
10 L/min for 8 hours (480 minutes) = **4 800 L**
Setting against the WPS
Setting − upper limit
WPS root 80–110 A, set at 118 A: **8 A** over

blocks.note: The circumference of a pipe is π × its outside diameter (π ≈ 3.142). Change hours to minutes before using a flow in L/min.

head: Hazard
What can happen
Control
rows: Ultraviolet radiation
TIG makes little smoke but very strong UV: arc eye and skin burns, even through thin shirts; UV reflects strongly off aluminium and stainless steel
Helmet with a suitable shade (often about 10–12 for most TIG currents, darker at high current), full skin cover, screens
Ozone and fume
UV turns oxygen in the air into ozone, which irritates the lungs; more on aluminium and at high current. Fume from stainless steel contains chromium compounds.
Extraction close to the arc; keep your head out of the plume; RPE where needed
Thoriated tungsten dust
Thoriated tungsten is slightly radioactive; breathing or swallowing its grinding dust is the main risk
Use lanthanated or ceriated where the WPS allows; grind on a dedicated grinder with extraction; collect and dispose of dust as the rules say
High-frequency (HF) starting
Electrical noise that upsets computers, card machines, CNC controls and phones nearby
Follow the maker's earthing advice; keep TIG leads short and apart from other cables; use lift-arc start near sensitive equipment
Argon in low or closed spaces
Argon has no smell or colour and is heavier than air. It collects in trenches, pits and tanks and pushes out the oxygen: a person can collapse without warning
Permits, oxygen testing before and during work, personal oxygen alarm, vent purge gas outside the space, forced ventilation, standby person
Electric shock
The tungsten and torch are live with the output on
Turn the output off before changing a tungsten; dry gloves; sound cables
Hot tungsten and filler
Burns
Let the tungsten cool before handling; put hot rod ends in a bin
Cleaning chemicals (pickling paste and gels)
Many contain nitric and hydrofluoric acids, which cause deep, dangerous burns and toxic fumes
Follow the SDS and the Centre's rules: acid-resistant gloves, eye and face protection, ventilation, neutralise and dispose of waste correctly; use electro-cleaning where allowed
Solvents for cleaning
Flammable; chlorinated solvents can form toxic gas in UV
Keep closed and away from the arc; let surfaces dry before welding; never use chlorinated solvents near welding

flow: Turn the machine output off (or switch the machine off)
Let the tungsten and torch cool
Remove the back cap and take out the tungsten
Fit the prepared tungsten at the right stick-out, and tighten the back cap
Turn the output back on and check the gas flow before striking

ul: Brief the WPS settings, the hazards and the controls at the job.
Check that screens are up: TIG UV burns the eyes of people passing by, even when the arc looks small.
Keep cylinders chained upright and closed when the job is finished.
When purging in trenches, tanks or pits, treat the space as a confined space and vent purge gas to the open air through a hose.

blocks.note: A trench in a hotel garden or a pump pit at a water-treatment works looks harmless. Argon from a purge or a leaking hose can settle in it within minutes on a still day. Test the air, vent the purge gas out, and never send someone down to "check" without the controls in place.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A modern inverter TIG set has many controls. Each one changes the arc, the pool or the tungsten in a way you can predict. Start from the WPS or the maker's chart, test on scrap of the same material and thickness, and change one setting at a time.

head: Setting
What it does
Typical use
rows: HF start
A high-frequency spark jumps the gap so the arc starts without touching
Clean starts with no tungsten contamination; avoid near sensitive electronics
Lift-arc start
The tungsten touches the work at low current, then lifts to start the arc
Where HF interference is a problem; DC work
Pre-flow
Gas flows for a moment before the arc starts
Clears air from the hose and the joint
Up-slope
Current rises gradually at the start
Gentle start on thin or crack-sensitive work
Down-slope (crater fill)
Current falls gradually at the end
Fills the crater and stops crater cracks
Post-flow
Gas keeps flowing after the arc stops
Protects the hot tungsten and the end of the weld; a common rule is about 1 second for every 10 A, with a sensible minimum
Foot pedal or torch control
Changes the current while welding
Reduce heat as the job heats up, as the position changes round a pipe, or at the end of a run

blocks.h: AC balance and AC frequency (for aluminium)

blocks.p: On AC the current switches direction many times a second. The **electrode-positive (EP)** part of each cycle breaks up the oxide skin (the **cleaning action**) but heats the tungsten. The **electrode-negative (EN)** part puts heat into the work for **penetration** and keeps the tungsten cool.

head: Control
Turn it towards more EP (more cleaning)
Turn it towards more EN (less cleaning)
rows: AC balance
Wider frosted cleaning band beside the weld
Hotter tungsten: it balls and may spit tungsten
Wider, shallower bead
Narrower, deeper bead; faster welding
Cooler tungsten; sharper point holds
Too far: oxide not removed, black specks and a dirty pool

head: Control
Higher setting
Lower setting
rows: AC frequency (often about 60–200 Hz on inverters)
Narrower, more focused arc that stays in the joint: good for fillets, corners and thin edges
Wider, softer arc: good for build-up and wide beads

blocks.note: Set only as much cleaning as the job needs: enough to give a clean, shiny pool with a thin frosted band. Inverter sets often start at about 65–75% EN; follow the WPS or the maker's chart.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: In **pulsed TIG** the current switches between a high **peak current** and a low **background current**. The peak melts a spot; the background lets the pool cool and freeze a little while the arc stays lit. You get good fusion with less total heat.

head: Pulse setting
What it controls
rows: Peak current
Fusion and penetration
Background current (often about 25–50% of peak)
How much the pool cools between pulses
Pulse rate (pulses per second)
Slow pulses (about 1–2 a second) give a rhythm for adding rod and a ripple pattern; fast pulses (100 or more a second) give a stiff, narrow arc
Peak time (% on peak)
How much of each pulse is at the high current: more peak time means more heat

ul: Use pulse on thin sheet, stainless steel, out-of-position welds, and wherever burn-through or distortion is a problem.
Start from the maker's guide and test on scrap; then record the settings that worked on the weld record.
**Air-cooled** torches suit lower currents and short runs. Long runs at high current (often over about 150–200 A) need a **water-cooled** torch, or the torch overheats.
The **cup** (nozzle) directs the gas. Cup sizes are often given as a number: the inside diameter in sixteenths of an inch (a No. 8 cup is about 12.7 mm).
A **gas lens** is a fine mesh in the collet body that smooths the gas into a steady, even stream. It gives better cover and lets you use a longer stick-out to reach into corners and roots.
Check the collet and collet body match the tungsten size, the back cap is tight, and the O-rings and hoses are sound.

blocks.p: On AC a tungsten carries less current than on DCEN. Too small a tungsten for the current overheats and melts; too large a tungsten gives a wandering arc at low current.

ul: Grind on a grinder or wheel kept **only for tungsten**, with extraction. A wheel used on steel puts steel into the tungsten.
Grind **lengthwise**, with the marks running along the tungsten towards the point. Marks round the tungsten make the arc wander.
The taper is usually about 2–2½ times the diameter long.
For higher currents, grind a tiny **flat** on the very tip so the fine point does not melt off into the weld.
A dipped or contaminated tungsten is broken back past the damage and reground.

head: Included angle at the point
Arc
Penetration
Tungsten life
rows: Sharper (smaller angle)
Wider, easier to start at low current
Shallower
Shorter
Blunter (larger angle)
Narrower, more focused
Deeper
Longer

blocks.p: **Stick-out** is the length of tungsten past the end of the cup. A normal cup often uses about 3–6 mm; a gas lens allows more to reach into roots and corners. Too long a stick-out without a gas lens leaves the tip outside the gas cover.

head: Gas
Effect
Use
rows: Argon
Easy starts, stable arc, good cleaning on AC, economical
Most TIG work
Argon-helium mixtures
Hotter arc, deeper penetration, faster travel; harder to start; needs more flow
Thick aluminium and copper
Argon for purging
Displaces air behind the root
Back purges, trailing shields

ul: Typical torch flow is often about 7–12 L/min of argon for normal cups; larger cups and gas lenses need more. Follow the WPS.
**More is not better**: too high a flow becomes turbulent and pulls air into the shield, causing porosity.
A **trailing shield** is a gas box fixed behind the torch. It keeps gas over the hot weld after the torch has passed, for reactive metals such as titanium, and for some stainless work.
Check hoses and fittings for leaks: a leaking fitting can suck air into the gas stream.

blocks.p: When the root of a stainless steel (or titanium) pipe weld is hot, the air inside the pipe attacks it. Without a purge the back of the root oxidises into a grey, crusty, rough layer called **sugaring**. It is weak, it traps dirt, and it has lost its resistance to corrosion, so the joint fails inspection and must be cut out. A **back purge** fills the inside with argon so the root comes out smooth and bright.

flow: Clean and line up the pipe ends and tack the joint
Fit **purge dams** inside the pipe each side of the joint (soluble paper dams, inflatable dams or plugs), close enough to keep the purged volume small
Tape over the joint gap so argon cannot escape and air cannot get in
Feed argon in through a hose at the flow the WPS gives, and let it out through a small **vent** (often on the far side or the top, since argon is heavier than air)
Purge long enough to change the gas several times (the WPS often gives a number of volume changes)
Check the vent with an **oxygen analyser**: welding starts only when the reading is below the limit the WPS gives
Peel the tape back only a little ahead of the weld as you go
Keep the purge on for the root and at least the next run, or as the WPS says

head: Sum
Worked example
rows: Purge time = volume changes × purged volume ÷ flow rate
5 changes × 3 L = 15 L; at 6 L/min: 15 ÷ 6 = **2.5 minutes**, then check with the analyser
Reading in % to ppm (parts per million)

blocks.note: The analyser decides when the purge is ready, not the clock. A sum gives the minimum time; leaks, a loose dam or a wet hose can mean it takes longer.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Fault
Result
Prevention
rows: Tape peeled too far ahead
Air gets in through the open gap: sugaring on that part of the root
Peel only a little at a time
Purge turned off straight after the root
The next run reheats the root, which oxidises
Keep the purge on for the next run
Purge flow too high, vent too small
Pressure inside pushes the root pool out or in, giving a concave or uneven root
Lower the flow once purged; make the vent big enough
Leaking hose or fitting
Air drawn into the purge; oxygen reading will not fall
Leak test; replace damaged parts
No oxygen check
Root may be oxidised although "the purge was on"
Always check at the vent

blocks.p: For a back-purged weld, the weld record also gives the **purge gas, its flow, the purge time and the oxygen reading** before welding, as well as the welder, settings and filler batch.

sections.title: Preparation, filler and technique in all positions

ul: Clean the joint and about 25 mm each side to bright metal, inside and out. Remove oil and marker ink with a clean solvent and a lint-free cloth, and let it dry.
Bevel and land (root face) as the WPS says; set an even root gap with a gap gauge or a spacer wire.
Tack with the same care as the root: small, fully fused tacks, feathered at their ends by grinding so the root can tie in.
On thin sheet, clamp a **copper backing bar** under the joint: copper draws heat away and supports the root without fusing to it.

head: Code
What it means
rows: ER
Electrode or rod: it can be used as a wire electrode (MIG) or a filler rod (TIG)
Minimum tensile strength of the weld metal, 70 000 psi (about 480 MPa)
S
Solid wire or rod
The chemistry group: -2 has extra deoxidisers and suits roots; -6 has more manganese and silicon for less-clean steel
Stainless fillers matching 304 and 316; L means low carbon, which protects corrosion resistance
Aluminium fillers: 4043 (aluminium-silicon) flows well and resists cracking; 5356 (aluminium-magnesium) is stronger and matches 5000-series plate

ul: Choose a rod diameter close to the metal thickness on thin work (for example 1.6 mm rod on 1.5–3 mm sheet), larger on thicker work.
Keep the hot end of the rod **inside the gas shield**. If the tip goes dark and oxidised, cut it off before you carry on, or the oxide goes into the weld.
Feed the rod into the **leading edge** of the pool; do not drip it from above or touch the tungsten with it.

blocks.p: On an open-root joint, a small hole called the **keyhole** forms at the front of the pool as the arc melts through both root faces. Keeping an even keyhole shows full penetration. Feed the rod into the keyhole so it fills the root and forms a small, even bead inside.

head: Method
How
Good for
rows: Walking the cup
Rest the cup on the joint edges and rock it from side to side to move along
Steady, even roots and caps on pipe, especially for long runs
Freehand
Hold the torch clear of the work, with a braced hand or finger
Thin sheet, fillets, and joints where the cup cannot rest
Lay-wire (fed wire)
The rod lies in the root gap and is melted in as the arc passes
Some pipe roots, as the WPS allows

head: Position (AWS)
Meaning
rows: 1G, 2G, 3G, 4G (plate)
Groove welds: flat, horizontal, vertical, overhead
1F, 2F, 3F, 4F (plate)
Fillet welds: flat, horizontal, vertical, overhead
1G (pipe)
Pipe axis horizontal, pipe rolled; welded at the top
2G (pipe)
Pipe axis vertical; weld runs round horizontally
5G (pipe)
Pipe axis horizontal and fixed; weld goes round through flat, vertical and overhead
6G (pipe)
Pipe fixed at 45°; the hardest test position

blocks.h: Welding fixed pipe (5G) from the bottom up

flow: Start each half just past the bottom (6 o'clock) and weld up to the top (12 o'clock)
Bottom (overhead): small pool, lower current, torch pointing up into the joint with a small push angle; feed rod into the keyhole so the root does not sag inside
Sides (vertical): change the torch angle to follow the pipe; current can rise a little; keep the keyhole even
Top (flat): the pipe is hotter, so reduce the heat with the pedal and add rod steadily to avoid burn-through
Move your body to stay comfortable; tie in carefully where the two halves meet at the top and bottom

ul: A **foot pedal** or torch control lets you change the heat as the position changes round the pipe.
Vertical-up fillets: point the torch up the joint, about 10–20° from square, and add rod at the leading edge.
Brace your hand and rest your arm where you can; keep the arc short and steady so the tungsten does not dip into the pool.

blocks.note: When a trainee keeps dipping the tungsten, do not tell them to hold a long arc or turn the current right down. Show them how to brace the torch hand, hold a short, steady arc, and feed the rod with the other hand without moving the torch.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Stainless steel, aluminium and other metals

blocks.p: Grades such as 304 and 316 carry heat away slowly and expand about half as much again as carbon steel when hot. Too much heat makes them warp badly, and holding them too hot for too long can form chromium carbides near the weld, which lowers their corrosion resistance. Heat also leaves coloured **heat tint**.

head: Control
Why
rows: Lowest current that gives full fusion; pulse if the machine has it
Less heat, less distortion and tint
Steady travel, small runs, no weaving wider than needed
Keeps heat input low
Close tacking and a balanced welding order
Holds the shape against shrinkage
Copper or aluminium chill bars
Draw heat away from thin sheet
Check interpass temperature and let the job cool between runs
Stops heat building up
Back purge for roots
Protects the inside from sugaring

head: Heat tint colour
Usually means
rows: Silver to light straw
Good gas cover; little oxide
Gold to brown
Some oxidation; may need cleaning, depending on the job's standard
Blue to purple
Heavier oxidation; poorer cover or too much heat
Grey, black, crusty (sugaring)
Badly oxidised; reject and cut out

ul: Keep stainless steel away from carbon steel: store it on wooden or plastic racks, and use **stainless-only** brushes, discs, clamps and tools. Iron particles from carbon steel rust and leave rust spots.

Remove heat tint by **pickling** or **electro-cleaning**, as the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules allow, so the steel regains its corrosion resistance. Grinding with a disc used on mild steel, or brushing with a carbon steel brush, makes it worse.
For food and drink work, welds must be smooth, fully fused and free of cracks, pits and crevices where dirt can hide.

head: Problem
Why
What to do
rows: Oxide skin
Aluminium oxide melts at about 2 050 °C, while aluminium melts at about 660 °C
Clean with solvent, then a stainless-only brush, just before welding; use AC for cleaning action
Black specks, dirty pool
Oxide or dirt left on, or too little cleaning (EP) in the balance
Clean better; add a little more cleaning
Porosity
Hydrogen from moisture, oil or damp oxide on the plate or rod
Clean, dry metal and rod; store rod in a dry, sealed tube; clean gloves
Pool slow to form on thick plate
Aluminium draws heat away very fast
Warm thick parts a little first, within the limit the WPS gives; use argon-helium; start with high current and reduce with the pedal
No colour change to warn you
Aluminium does not glow before it melts
Watch for the pool to go wet and shiny before adding rod

blocks.note: Some aluminium alloys are heat treated for strength and lose it if preheated too hot or for too long. Follow the WPS limit and check with a crayon or thermometer.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Copper** carries heat away very fast: thick parts need preheat and a hotter arc (argon-helium, DCEN).

**Titanium** is light and strong, used in aircraft and chemical plants. Hot titanium takes up oxygen and nitrogen from the air and becomes brittle, so it needs full gas cover: a trailing shield on top and a purge underneath until it has cooled.

Main causes
Found by
Prevention

Looking inside (mirror, borescope); radiography

Too much heat or too wide a gap
Looking inside; radiography
Correct gap; less heat, especially at the top of a pipe
Concave root (suck-back)
Too much heat or too little filler, mostly at the bottom of a fixed pipe; purge pressure too high
Looking inside; radiography
Feed enough rod into the keyhole overhead; control heat; lower purge pressure

No purge, poor purge or purge turned off too soon
Looking inside
Purge to the WPS oxygen level and keep it on

Tungsten dipped in the pool or touched by the rod; current too high for the tungsten
Radiography: a bright white spot
Steady hand; right current and tungsten size; regrind after a dip
Porosity
Poor gas cover (draughts, wrong flow, leaks), dirty metal or rod, hydrogen on aluminium
By eye; radiography
Clean metal and rod; right flow; screen draughts
Crater crack
Arc stopped suddenly at the end of a run
By eye; dye penetrant
Use down-slope or the pedal to taper off; add rod as the crater closes
Centreline crack
Thin, concave bead from too little filler; high restraint
By eye; dye penetrant
Add enough filler for a slightly convex bead
Lack of side-wall fusion

Radiography, ultrasonic testing, bend tests

head: Method
What it shows
Notes
rows: Visual inspection (VT)
Profile, size, surface defects, heat tint
Every weld, in good light, inside and out where possible
Mirror or borescope
The inside of a pipe root: penetration, smooth profile, no sugaring
Essential on food-grade and purged stainless pipe
Dye penetrant (PT)
Fine cracks and pores open to the surface on any non-porous metal
Used on aluminium and stainless steel, which are not magnetic
Radiography (RT)
Internal defects: pores (dark spots), lack of penetration (dark line), tungsten (white spots)
Licensed operators and a cleared area
Bend tests, macro-etch, nick-break
Fusion and soundness through the weld
Destructive: used on test pieces and procedure trials
Hydrostatic (water pressure) test
That a finished pipe system holds its test pressure without leaking
Done after NDT, to the pressure and time the specification gives

ul: Weld record: weld number, welder ID, WPS, settings used (current, gas flow, tungsten), filler batch, base metal heat number, date.
Purge record for purged welds: gas, flow, time, oxygen reading.
Inspection results, with any repairs.
Certificates for filler and plate, kept with the job file.
Close the cylinder valves and bleed the lines; switch off and isolate the machine.
Put tungstens and rod offcuts away labelled by type, and hot rod ends in a bin.
Return unused stainless and aluminium to their separate racks.
Leave the area clean and safe, and report any faults.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can explain when TIG is the best process, and why it is used for pipe roots.
I can choose the current type, gas, tungsten and filler for carbon steel, stainless steel, aluminium, copper and titanium.
I can explain how a WPS is trialled and approved with a PQR, and how welders are qualified.
I can work out heat input, welding time round a pipe, gas use and how far a setting is outside the WPS.
I can control UV, ozone, tungsten dust, HF interference, argon build-up and cleaning chemicals.
I can set pre-flow, slope, post-flow and the pedal, and explain AC balance, AC frequency and pulse.
I can choose, grind and fit a tungsten, and explain the effect of the point angle and stick-out.
I can set the gas flow, and explain gas lenses, helium mixtures and trailing shields.
I can set up a back purge with dams, tape and a vent, and check it with an oxygen analyser.
I can weld an open root with a keyhole, walk the cup, and weld a fixed pipe from the bottom up.
I can control heat and contamination on stainless steel and clean its heat tint safely.
I can deal with oxide and porosity on aluminium.
I can name TIG defects, their causes, how they are found and how to prevent them.
I can choose inspection and test methods and keep the weld and purge records.
I can coach a trainee and check the team's work against the WPS.

terms: The share of each AC cycle spent electrode-positive (cleaning) or electrode-negative (penetration)
A weld made by melting the edges together with no filler rod
Argon fed inside a pipe or behind a joint to protect the back of the root
Direct current, electrode negative: most of the heat goes into the work
A gradual fall in current at the end of a run, to fill the crater
Electrode or rod: the start of a solid filler code such as ER70S-2
A fine mesh in the torch that gives a smooth, even gas stream
The energy put into the weld per millimetre, in kJ/mm
The band of colours left on stainless steel beside a weld
High frequency: a spark used to start the arc without touching
A small hole at the front of the pool showing full root penetration
The thin, tough skin on aluminium that must be cleaned and broken up
Gas that keeps flowing after the arc stops
Current switching between a peak and a background level
A plug or soluble paper dam inside a pipe that holds the purge gas near the weld
The length of tungsten that sticks out past the end of the cup
A grey, crusty, oxidised root on stainless steel caused by a poor purge
A concave root that sinks inside the pipe
A gas box behind the torch that keeps gas over the hot weld
Bits of tungsten trapped in the weld; white spots on a radiograph
Rocking the cup on the joint edges to move along the weld

c1.title: Food-grade stainless pipe at a dairy near Claremont
c1.text: Rohan's team is TIG welding 304L stainless steel milk pipe at a dairy near Claremont, St Ann. The WPS calls for a back purge with argon and an oxygen reading below 200 ppm at the vent before welding. On the first joint, a trainee peeled all the tape off the gap before starting, and the last 40 mm of the root has come out grey and crusty inside. The trainee also wants to turn the purge off as soon as each root is finished, to save argon. The plant engineer asks how the finished line will be proved.

c2.title: An aluminium fuel tank in Port Royal
c2.text: Sanjay is TIG welding a fuel tank of 6 mm 5083 aluminium plate for a fishing boat in Port Royal, on an AC inverter with pure argon. The WPS calls for ER5356 filler. His first welds show a frosted band about 8 mm wide each side, and the tungsten has balled up and spat into the pool. On the inside-corner fillets the arc wanders from one plate to the other. Before welding, he wiped the plate with a rag from the box of shop rags used on engines, and the welds show porosity.

c3.title: Boiler feed pipe in Harbour View
c3.text: Odane is welding carbon steel boiler feed pipe, 88.9 mm outside diameter, fixed in the 5G position at a factory in Harbour View, Kingston. The WPS gives a GTAW root with ER70S-2 at 85–110 A, then MMAW fill and cap. Radiographs of his first joint show a concave root near the bottom of the pipe, excess penetration near the top, and one small bright white spot. His team leader notices his root current is set at 118 A. He welds the root at about 70 mm a minute.

c4.title: A stainless kitchen hood in Mandeville
c4.text: Keisha is TIG welding a kitchen hood from 1.2 mm grade 304 stainless sheet for a restaurant in Mandeville, Manchester, using pulsed DC. Her root runs average about 10 V and 75 A at about 200 mm a minute. The first panel buckled badly along the seams. The heat tint is to be removed with a pickling paste whose label lists nitric acid and hydrofluoric acid.

c5.title: The tungsten tray at a centre in Hopewell
c5.text: At a training centre in Hopewell, Hanover, the WPS for a stainless job lists 2% lanthanated tungsten. The tray at the TIG bay holds loose, unlabelled tungstens with red, grey, gold and blue bands. A trainee is sharpening his tungsten on the general bench grinder, turning it so the marks run round it. Another trainee is welding 1 mm sheet at about 30 A with a 3.2 mm tungsten, and her arc keeps wandering.

questions.q: The analyser at the vent reads 0.1% oxygen. May welding start?
o: Yes: 0.1% is far below the 200 ppm limit
No: 0.1% is 1 000 ppm, so keep purging
Yes: any reading under 1% is good enough
No: the reading must be exactly 0 ppm first
questions.why: One per cent is 10 000 ppm, so 0.1% is 1 000 ppm, five times the WPS limit. Keep purging, check for leaks at the dams and tape, and start only when the reading is below 200 ppm.

questions.q: What caused the grey, crusty end of the first root, and how is it prevented?
o: Too little filler: add more rod to the last part of the root
Too high a current: turn it down as the joint heats up
Air came in at the open gap: peel the tape back bit by bit
Dirty filler rod: wipe each rod with solvent before using it
questions.why: With the whole gap open, air entered and the hot root oxidised (sugaring). Peeling the tape back only a short way ahead of the weld keeps the argon in. The sugared root cannot be cleaned to an acceptable standard and is cut out.

questions.q: How should Rohan answer the trainee who wants to switch the purge off after each root?
o: Agree: once the root is made, the inside is already protected
Agree, as long as he waits five minutes after the root
Disagree: turn the purge up higher for the cap instead
Disagree: the next run reheats the root, so keep the purge on
questions.why: The second run heats the root again to a temperature at which it oxidises. The purge stays on for the root and at least the next run, or as the WPS says.

questions.q: Which test proves that the finished milk line holds pressure without leaking?
o: Dye penetrant testing on every weld
A borescope check inside each root
Radiography of a sample of the welds
A water pressure (hydrostatic) test
questions.why: A hydrostatic test fills the line with water and holds it at the specified pressure and time, proving the whole system is tight. PT, borescope and radiography inspect welds, but none of them proves the line holds pressure.

questions.q: What change to the AC balance should Sanjay make?
o: Less electrode-positive time, for less cleaning
More electrode-positive time, for more cleaning
Set the balance to 50% so each half is the same
Leave the balance and change to a pure tungsten
questions.why: A wide frosted band and a hot, spitting tungsten show too much electrode-positive (cleaning) time. Moving the balance towards electrode-negative gives a narrower band, deeper penetration and a cooler tungsten, while still cleaning enough.

questions.q: What setting helps keep the arc in the inside corners?
o: A lower AC frequency, to spread the arc wider
A higher AC frequency, to narrow and focus the arc
A higher gas flow, to push the arc into the corner
A longer arc length, so it can reach both plates
questions.why: Raising the AC frequency gives a narrower, stiffer arc that stays where it is pointed, which helps in fillets and corners. A lower frequency gives a wider, softer arc.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the porosity?
o: Hydrogen from oil left on the plate by the shop rag
The AC frequency is set higher than the maker's guide
The tungsten has been ground to a point, not balled
ER5356 filler is always porous on 5083 plate
questions.why: Oil, grease and moisture break down in the arc and release hydrogen, which aluminium takes up and then traps as pores. Clean with a fresh solvent and a lint-free cloth, then a stainless-only brush, just before welding.

questions.q: Why does the WPS call for ER5356 rather than ER4043 on this plate?
o: ER5356 melts at a much lower heat, so it is easier to use
ER5356 is stronger and matches 5000-series plate like 5083
ER5356 needs no cleaning of the oxide before it is used
ER5356 can be welded on DCEN without any AC cleaning
questions.why: ER5356 is an aluminium-magnesium filler that gives a stronger weld and matches 5000-series plate such as 5083, used in boats and tanks. ER4043 flows well but gives a weaker joint on these alloys.

questions.q: What most likely caused the concave root near the bottom of the pipe?
o: Too little heat with too much filler in the overhead part
Too much heat and too little filler in the overhead part
A root gap that was set far too small at the bottom
A gas flow that was set too low at the start of the run
questions.why: At the bottom of a fixed pipe, gravity pulls an over-large, under-filled pool away from the inside, leaving a concave root (suck-back). Keep the pool small, use less heat overhead, and feed enough rod into the keyhole.

questions.q: What is the small bright white spot on the radiograph, and how is it prevented?
o: A gas pore: increase the flow of argon at the torch
A crack: use down-slope at the end of every run
Tungsten from a dip: regrind after any touch
Slag: clean between every run with a wire brush
questions.why: Tungsten is much denser than steel, so it shows white on the film, while pores and lack of penetration show dark. A dipped or touched tungsten must be broken back and reground before welding goes on.

questions.q: What should the team leader do about the 118 A root setting?
o: Let him carry on, as 8 A over is close enough
Ask the office to change the WPS to 85–120 A
Stop, reset within range and check his finished roots
Tell him to keep 118 A for the root and use less on the cap
questions.why: The setting is 8 A above the WPS range, and the excess penetration at the top fits too much heat. Welding stops, the current is reset within range, and the roots already made are checked. Only an authorised person changes a WPS.

questions.q: About how long should Odane take to weld one root right round the pipe?
o: About 1.3 minutes
About 4 minutes
About 8 minutes
About 20 minutes
questions.why: Circumference = π × 88.9 ≈ 3.142 × 88.9 ≈ 279 mm. At 70 mm a minute: 279 ÷ 70 ≈ 4 minutes. Dividing the diameter (not the circumference) by the speed gives the wrong 1.3 minutes.

questions.q: What is the heat input of Keisha's root runs?
o: About 0.02 kJ/mm
About 0.23 kJ/mm
About 0.75 kJ/mm
About 2.3 kJ/mm

questions.q: Which change will most reduce the buckling on the next panel?
o: Weld each seam in one long run at higher current to finish sooner
Use fewer tacks so the sheet can move freely as it is welded
Close tacks, chill bars and short runs in a balanced order
Cool each seam with a wet rag straight after welding it
questions.why: Stainless sheet holds heat and expands a lot, so control the heat and hold the shape: close tacking, copper or aluminium chill bars, low pulsed heat, short runs and a balanced order, letting it cool between runs.

questions.q: How should the pickling paste be used?
o: Spread it with bare fingers so it can be worked into the tint
Use it in a closed room so the fumes cannot reach anyone
Wash it off down the floor drain with plenty of water
As its SDS says: acid-proof gloves, face shield, airflow
questions.why: Hydrofluoric acid causes deep burns that may not hurt at first, and the paste gives off harmful fumes. Follow the SDS: acid-resistant gloves, eye and face protection, good ventilation, and neutralise and dispose of the waste as the rules say.

questions.q: How should the trainee sharpen his tungsten?
o: Lengthwise, on a wheel kept only for tungsten
Round its circumference, on any clean bench wheel
With a file, so it does not overheat at the tip
By dipping it in the pool to melt it into a point
questions.why: Marks running round the tungsten make the arc wander, and a general wheel puts steel into the tungsten. Grind lengthwise, with the marks towards the point, on a dedicated wheel with extraction.

questions.q: Which tungstens in the tray most likely match the WPS?
o: The red-banded ones
The grey-banded ones
The gold-banded ones
The blue-banded ones
questions.why: On most boxes (the ISO code), blue is 2% lanthanated, gold 1.5% lanthanated, grey ceriated and red thoriated. Because the tray is unlabelled and colours can vary, take tungstens from a labelled box and sort the tray.

questions.q: Why does the second trainee's arc keep wandering?
o: The 3.2 mm tungsten is too big for 30 A
The current is too high for 1 mm sheet
The tungsten has been ground too sharp
The argon flow is set at the usual rate
questions.why: At low current a large tungsten tip does not get hot enough to hold a steady arc spot, so the arc wanders. A 1.0 mm or 1.6 mm tungsten suits about 30 A.

questions.q: Courtney sets 25 L/min of argon on a standard cup indoors, saying more gas gives better cover. His welds show porosity. Why?
o: Argon at that flow is too cold and freezes the pool
Turbulent flow draws air into the shield
The cylinder empties too fast to keep any pressure
High flow lifts the tungsten out of the collet
questions.why: Too much flow turns the smooth gas stream turbulent, so it mixes with the air around it. Set the flow the WPS gives, often about 7–12 L/min for a normal cup, and screen draughts.

questions.q: A TIG weld on a titanium bracket comes out dull blue-white and powdery. What does this show?
o: Normal heat tint, which polishes off easily
The filler rod was too thin for the joint
It was not shielded until cool: reject it
The current was too low for the thickness
questions.why: Hot titanium takes up oxygen and nitrogen and becomes brittle. Dull blue, white or powdery colours show it was exposed while hot. It needs a trailing shield and a back purge until it cools, and a weld like this is rejected.
